A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, renamed from RAP-SAM to RMP-SAM. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation benchmarks, component and co-training ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative analyses, including additional experiments in Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds SAM comparisons, GPU-platform measurements, stronger video-model comparisons, and attention visualizations in Sections 4 and 7.

M1.justification: The feature extractor, shared dynamic-convolution decoder, asymmetric adapters, losses, CLIP classifier, and query-matching inference remain unchanged. The renaming and additional fine-tuning experiments do not establish a revised core algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 introduces SAM-data training for the promptable-segmentation comparison, specifically fine-tuning on 10% of that dataset in Section 7.1. v1 explicitly excluded SAM data from training. This substantially expands training-data coverage; COCO, YouTube-VIS 2019, ADE20K, and VIPSeg remain the evaluation datasets.

E2.justification: The SAM-H-only promptable comparison expands to TinySAM, MobileSAM, EdgeSAM, EfficientSAM, and FastSAM. v2 also adds SAM-L and Semantic-SAM-L to the single-click comparison and UniVS, DVIS, and Tube-Link to the stronger YouTube-VIS comparison. SAM-2 is discussed but not numerically evaluated.

E3.justification: The stated main training budget changes from 24 to 12 epochs, without establishing that the retained results were rerun. New protocols include SAM prompt-branch fine-tuning and YouTube-VIS-specific fine-tuning. Detector comparisons replace the earlier X-101 setting with ResNet101 and ViTDet-B settings, add object-size AP metrics, and extend timing beyond A100 to A10 and RTX 3090.

E4.justification: v2 adds a four-frame attention-map case study examining task behavior under the shared decoder (Figure 6) and an efficiency check across GPU platforms (Table 13). The original architecture, adapter, co-training, adapter-transfer, and failure-case analyses are substantially retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The numerical entries in Table 3 and the matched extended-backbone and adapter-transfer tables are retained. v2 adds substantial results, including SAM-trained mask AP of 33.5 and 41.0 with different detectors (Tables 10 and 12), and video results under additional training settings (Table 14); these are not same-setting gains over v1. It also removes temporal-window VPQ breakdowns, ADE20K thing/stuff PQ breakdowns, and shared-decoder ablation FPS values.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(5), the loss formulation, and the mathematical task descriptions retain their substance. The prompt-coordinate example changes from boxes to points, both already supported. Neither version adds theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive derivations.

C1.justification: The central claims about a unified real-time model, asymmetric adapters, and favorable speed-accuracy trade-offs remain. v2 adds an introductory claim of competitive performance after SAM-data training. Renaming all-purpose segmentation to multi-purpose segmentation does not itself change the claimed task scope.

C2.justification: Section 7.2 newly qualifies that multi-task training may not produce the best single-task performance against specialized video models. v2 also removes v1's point-only limitation, although v1 already described and evaluated box prompting elsewhere. The overlap/crowding failure explanations and principal adapter rationale remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses homogeneous data types within batches, a 1:25:1 dataset-sampling ratio, mask-center testing prompts, SAM fine-tuning details, and exact GPU variants. The optimizer and augmentation details were already in v1's appendix. MMDetection identification is omitted, while the repository address remains; an implementation replacement is not established.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning through a detailed SAM-2 comparison, discussion of specialized video methods, and an interactive-segmentation subsection citing works such as FocalClick and RITM. It removes the dedicated vision-foundation-model subsection and associated citations. These changes go beyond bibliography formatting or publication updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, terminology changes throughout, and related work moves from before the method to after the experiments. The supplementary material becomes a reorganized numbered appendix after the references, with separate method-details, results, visualization, and limitations sections.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column layout and extensively reorganizes displays. Figure 1 gains interactive-segmentation plots; new figures show SAM efficiency comparisons and attention maps. Existing benchmark tables are regrouped, transfer and ablation tables are merged, and retained qualitative figures are relocated. Figure 4 also loses one video example.

improvement.justification: v2 provides more relevant evidence for the efficiency claims through efficient-SAM baselines, stronger video comparisons, multiple GPU measurements, and additional training disclosures. These improve assessment of competitiveness and deployment limits. However, reporting problems temper the gains: Table 4 names Faster R-CNN while Section 4.1 names Mask R-CNN, and its noninteractive marking for SAM contradicts Table 2. The additions therefore support a useful but limited net improvement.
